questions.question: A sales rep clicks "Submit" and must see the external system's response (success or failure) on screen before moving on. Which integration style fits best?
options: Remote Process Invocation – Request and Reply (synchronous)
Fire and Forget (asynchronous, no reply expected)
Batch Data Synchronization
Remote Call-In with no response handling
questions.explanation: Whenever a human is waiting for an immediate yes/no answer, you need a synchronous request-reply call — the caller blocks until the response comes back.

questions.question: Which statement best describes 'Fire and Forget'?
options: The caller sends a request and does not wait for or care about an immediate response
The caller sends a request and polls repeatedly until a response arrives
Two systems exchange full data dumps on a nightly schedule
An external system calls into Salesforce and waits for Salesforce to respond
questions.explanation: Fire and Forget is asynchronous and one-directional: the sender moves on immediately and assumes the receiver will handle the message (or doesn't need a result).

questions.question: An external order system needs to be notified in near-real time, for every single record, whenever an Opportunity closes in Salesforce. Which pattern is the best fit?
options: Batch Data Synchronization on a nightly schedule
Event-driven integration using a Platform Event or Change Data Capture
A once-a-week manual CSV export
Remote Call-In, where the order system polls Salesforce every 24 hours
questions.explanation: Per-record, near-real-time notification without the receiver having to poll is exactly what event-driven integration (Platform Events / CDC) is designed for.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of choosing Batch Data Synchronization over a real-time pattern?
options: Batch is always more expensive to build than real-time
Data will be stale between sync runs, but the approach is simpler and easier on API limits
Batch cannot move more than one record at a time
Batch requires the external system to expose a SOAP API
questions.explanation: Batch jobs trade immediacy for simplicity and efficiency — you accept that data is only as fresh as the last run, in exchange for fewer moving parts and lower API usage.

questions.question: Why is it useful to name an integration pattern (e.g. 'Request and Reply') before writing any code?
options: It has no real benefit, it's just terminology
It forces you to clarify who initiates the call, whether a reply is required, and the timing — which drives your technical design
It is required by Salesforce's API documentation
It automatically generates the Apex code for you
questions.explanation: Naming the pattern is a design step: it pins down direction, synchronicity, and volume expectations before you pick a specific technology (REST, SOAP, Platform Events, etc.).
